summary:
The Republic of Tyva (Tuva) stands under the national framework of Russia, and the source inventory contains no division-specific transgender evidence for this republic. A trans visitor to Tuva is therefore assessed against the countrywide regime as it operates there.

Russia presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors, and the position has hardened since 2022. Consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised, but same-sex marriage and legal gender recognition are banned: the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and gender changes on official documents was signed in 2023, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year. The Supreme Court of Russia designated the international LGBT+ movement an extremist organisation in November 2023. The expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that includes, explicitly, anything justifying gender transition. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, up to 15 days' detention and deportation, and the US State Department advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, with warnings directed at LGBT travellers.

The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) is the framework this republic is assessed against. It records that between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement, that 'gay propaganda' fines for individuals reach 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or 15 days' detention, and that the note carries no information specific to Tuva beyond the national framework. The same Home Office policy affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, which sets the standard for UK asylum claims.

Human Rights Watch reported on 30 June 2025 that Russian courts had issued 101 extremism-related convictions for participation in the designated International LGBT Movement or for displaying its symbols since the November 2023 ruling, with defendants facing up to 12 years in prison. It also documented 81 people found guilty in 98 cases since January 2024 of administrative offences under article 20.3 for displaying banned LGBT symbols, mostly on social media. That article carries no Tuva-specific detail; it sets the national enforcement baseline against which Tuva is scored, and Human Rights Watch has called on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Enforcement is escalating in volume as well as severity. Cases under the propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines under those statutes brought more than 60 million rubles into the state budget in the two years preceding June 2025. Within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's designation, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars, where about 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, while at least two other venues were raided the same night.

Physical coercion against transgender people is documented. In July 2024 the BBC followed a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk, where she was held for nine months and forced to take testosterone, pray and perform manual labour before escaping. In December 2024 a Russian man detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel agency was found dead in a pretrial detention facility.
tangentialFactors:
The enforcement pattern visible in the inventory is concentrated in the large western cities: the documented bar raids occurred in Moscow, and the administrative symbol-display cases were largely brought over social media posts rather than physical conduct. Exposure in Tuva is therefore driven at least as much by online activity and device checks as by any local venue, since no LGBTQ+ venues or community spaces in this republic are recorded in the sources.

The autonomous republic of Chechnya is named in the UK Home Office note as an example of a Russian subnational unit where LGBT+ people are recognised as a particular social group for refugee purposes, indicating that conditions are understood to vary between Russian regions while the national legal regime applies everywhere. No comparable regional reporting exists for Tuva.

Neighbouring Kazakhstan and Mongolia are not referenced in the inventory in relation to exit routes or asylum pathways for trans people leaving Russia, and no cross-border comparison for this republic is sourced.
localsOnly:
Residents of Tuva cannot obtain legal gender recognition: the 2023 law bars gender changes on official documents and prohibits gender reassignment surgery, and trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned the same year. Residents live under the same extremism designation, propaganda provisions and administrative penalties as visitors, with individual 'gay propaganda' fines reaching 400,000 rubles or 15 days' detention.

Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals across Russia were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement, and 101 extremism-related convictions had been issued by 30 June 2025, carrying sentences of up to 12 years. A further 81 people were found guilty in 98 administrative cases under article 20.3 since January 2024, most concerning banned symbols displayed online.

Residents who flee Russia may rely on the UK Home Office position that LGBT+ people in Russia constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, and Human Rights Watch has urged governments to offer safe haven. No Tuva-specific support services, community organisations or legal aid providers for trans residents appear in the inventory.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Tuva-specific enforcement data, arrest records or incident reports concerning transgender people are sourced for this republic; the assessment rests entirely on the national framework, and the UK Home Office note itself contains no Tuva-specific information.

Whether Tyva's own regional legislation adds restrictions beyond the federal statutes, and whether local police practice differs from the Moscow and St Petersburg pattern, is unresolved in the inventory.

The availability of gender-affirming care, document-change procedures in practice, and any LGBTQ+ venues or support networks within Tuva are not sourced and remain unknown.

The eighteenfold growth in propaganda cases and the 60 million rubles in fines are national aggregates with no regional breakdown, so their distribution across Tuva is unresolved.
